Introduction To CSS at whoaverse

This is not really a complete introduction.

I assume that you understand the basics of HTML and how CSS properties and styles work -

or you that you look them up yourself.

A CSS stylesheet is a set of CSS style rules that are applied to HTML pages.

Each rule has two parts - a list of selectors and a set of declarations.

The format for each rule is:

< SELECTORS> { < DECLARATIONS> }

Selectors

Usually there is a single selector...

a { padding: 5px; }

...but you can also have a list separated by commas - ,

a, .sitelisting, #header { border: 0;}

There are 3 types of selectors and each has a different purpose:

Element selectors

These are applied to all the HTML elements on the page that match the selector.

Each element selector name is the same as the matching HTML element.

The point of an element selector is that you can apply the style to specific HTML elements - e.g. all links < a>

a, p, div, span { color: black; background-color: white }

all the < a> , < p>, < div> and < span> HTML elements will have black text on a white background.

Note:

I had to enter the examples with a space between the < and the element name - < a>.

You cannot use HTML in comments so this is just a workaround to be able to give some examples

Class selectors

These are applied to any and all HTML tags that specify the class name in their class property.

Class selectors all start with a .

The point of a class selector is that you can apply the style to many different HTML elements.

.side, .content { font-weight: bold; }

All HTML elements with class='side' or class='content' will have bold text

< div class='side' ...>

ID selectors

These are applied to any the HTML element that has the given id

id selectors all start with a #

The point of an id selector is that you can apply the style to one specific HTML element on a page.

Each HTML element can have an id property (which should be unique on a page)

Browsers don't actually care though - it's up to you to make sure the ids are unique.

#header { display: none; }

The HTML element that has id='header' is removed

< div id='header' ...>

Selectors can be much more complex though.

For a more thorough overview - see the wikipedia page on CSS selectors

Some of the more common complex selectors:

Combine 2 selectors together - like element and class: element.class

This will only apply the styles to the single HTML element with the specified class name

li.selected { border: solid 1px red; }

This draw a thin red line around all li elements with the selected class

< li class='selected' ...> elements

Notes:

  • There is NO space between the element name and the class name!

  • In fact you can combine any 2 selector types together but most other combinations have no meaning

    .comment.deleted { display:none; }

All HTML elements that have both classes defined are removed

< div class="comment deleted" ...> - MATCHES and is removed
< div class="comment" ...> - DOESN'T MATCH and remains

Combine 2 selectors as parent and child together - like and id with an element #id .element

This selects all the elements that match the first selector and from those it selects only those that match the second selector too.

The second selector only selects elements nested inside the selected elements in the HTML document.

.md h1, .md h2, .md h3, .md h4{ margin:1em; font-weight:bold }

This adds padding and makes the text bold to all heading elements (< h1>, < h2>, < h3>, < h4>)

that are inside any element with the md class

< div class='md'>
 < h1>Rules:< /h1> ...
< /div>

The second selector can be nested even deeper

< div class='md'>
 < div class='expando'>
 < h1>Rules:< /h1> ...
 < /div> ...
< /div>

Notes:

  • There IS a space between the first selector and the second!

  • Selectors can be combined and nested as deep as you like as long as the nesting relationship is in the HTML document

    .tabmenu li.selected a { border-color:#696 }

Delarations

A single declaration looks like...

property : value ;

for example a declaration for link elements is

a {border: solid orange 5px}

...but most rules have a list separated by semi colons ;

.commentarea h1 { padding-top: 0.4em; font-size: 150%;}

It's generally a good idea to use the following format for rules

.commentarea h1 { <----- The selector and opening brace on the first line
 padding-top: 0.4em; <----- each delcaration has its own line...
 font-size: 150%; <----- .. and includes the semi-colon at the end
 } <----- The closing brace on the last line

The browser doesn't care, but it makes it easier to read for humans if the selectors appear on the first line with the opening brace {

and each declaration has it's own line with a semi-colon at the end. Finally the closing brace } ends the rule

(Yes I broke those rules in my examples)

There are a few things worth mentioning about declarations but you should really read up about them on your own

Colors

  • You can specify colors by name

    color: pink;

  • You can use the hex code (upper or lower case letters are OK)

    color: #FFC0CB;

You can save characters by using a shorthand 3 character hex code

color: #eae; is equivalent to
color: #eeaaee;

  • You can make them transparent:

    background-color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5);

This gives a black background color with 50% transparency.

These use decimal numbers between 0 and 255 for the color part and a number between 0 and 1 for the transparency.

Each can also be given using %values

background-color: rgba(75%, 75%, 75%, 10%);

A light grey background that's 10% transparent

  • See more details at the W3C's website

Images

Images must be hosted on another site - Imgur is a great place to do that

You give the location using the url function

background-image:url([http://i.imgur.com/aaa.jpg](http://i.imgur.com/aaa.jpg));

Again - check the W3C's site for the exact syntax and notes
